## Paper

## Abstract

Aqueous microdroplets have fascinated scientists with unique properties that deviate from bulk solutions. Understanding microdroplet chemistry has been limited by few spectroscopic measurements on single well-defined microdroplets. Here we present a new technique to record an IR spectrum of a single droplet called Single Droplet Displacement Infrared Action Spectroscopy (SiDDIRAS) with potential broad applications in physical, analytical, and environmental chemistry. The droplet was trapped in a linear quadrupole electrodynamic balance. When IR radiation at resonant frequency was introduced, mass loss from IR-induced evaporation caused the droplet to displace upwards. Mapping the displacement as a function of IR frequency yields an IR spectrum of a single microdroplet. As a demonstration, the SiDDIRA spectrum of an ~8 µm droplet containing NaCl and NaN3 shows that the azide asymmetric stretch blueshifts by 5 cm-1 relative to bulk with significant peak broadening, evidence that this droplet is supersaturated with salts compared to bulk solutions.

---

## Introduction

Electrospray ionization (ESI) remains a popular method to introduce ions and charged biomolecules to a mass spectrometer for analysis since its invention in the 1960s.1 Yet the complex ionization process from charged droplets to charged ions continues to be a topic of active research.2, 3 More recently, using ESI and pneumatic sprays, studies by several groups have reported enhanced chemical reactivity in microdroplets.4, 5, 6, 7, 8 More broadly, chemistry occurring in droplets and aerosol particles in the environment has great impact on atmospheric chemistry and climate.9

The electrodynamic balance is a class of instruments that have been used to study microdroplets for decades. In recent years, the linear quadrupole electrodynamic balance (LQ-EDB) has become popular.10 The LQ-EDB laterally confines charged droplets by applying AC voltages to four cylindrical rods held in a quadrupole configuration (Figure 4A, vide infra) while balancing gravity on the droplet with a DC voltage (Figure 4B, vide infra). The LQ-EDB is held in an environmentally controlled chamber and can be coupled with various optical techniques to obtain physical information such as radius,11 refractive index (RI),12 hygroscopicity,13 and viscosity.14 Specifically, in our set up, a broadband LED is used to collect back-scattered light with characteristic whispering gallery modes (WGMs) from the droplet to determine its radius and RI simultaneously (left in Figure 4A, vide in fra), as described previously12 and in more detail in Section S1.2 in the Supporting Information (SI). The chemical composition of the droplet can also be obtained by coupling the LQ-EDB with Raman13, 15 or fluorescence16 spectroscopies and mass spectrometry,17, 18, 19 further highlighting the versatility of the instrument.

Among these techniques, the use of IR spectroscopy for measuring single droplets has been limited, despite its potential for revealing the unique chemical microenvironment of the droplets, especially its sensitivity to changes in the hydrogen bonding network of water. Traditional FTIR measurements are not possible with trapped micron-sized droplets due to scattering and the small optical path length. IR spectroscopy studies based on optical photothermal effects have been reported for droplets deposited on a substrate,20, 21, 22 but the droplet-substrate interface might interfere with droplet chemistry. Additionally, the charge state and radius of such droplet is difficult to determine. To overcome these challenges, we report a new type of IR “action” spectroscopy, the principle of which has provided, and continues to provide, deep chemical and physical insights in the gas-phase community for the past few decades.23, 24, 25, 26, 27

Action IR spectroscopy on aerosol particles trapped in an EDB were first introduced by several groups in the 1980s. Arnold et al.28, 29 described a technique called Structure Resonance Molecular Spectroscopy (SRMS), where the authors induced an ammonium sulfate droplet’s evaporation at a certain IR frequency using an SiC Glo-Bar. The fractional change in a droplet’s scattering pattern upon resonant IR-induced evaporation is then fitted with Mie theory and mapped as a function of IR frequency to produce an IR spectrum. Lin30 followed with a method for measuring an action IR spectrum of solid particles, where the photophoretic force acting on a trapped solid ammonium sulfate particle upon absorbing IR photons from a CO laser displaced the particle from its original position. Thus, by measuring the fractional change in balancing voltage required to bring the particle back to its original position (ΔV/V) and mapping it to the IR frequency, an action spectrum was obtained.

Based on these seminal works, we described below an action IR technique for aqueous microdroplets in a LQ-EDB that does not require complex Mie fittings, as shown in Arnold et al.’s works.28, 29 In a way, our detection method is more similar to that described by Lin30 in that we are using the droplet’s displacement from its original position in our measurement. However, we want to stress that we are not measuring the photophoretic force acting on the droplet nor the fractional voltage to bring the droplet back to its original position. Instead, we are mapping the magnitude of the droplet’s displacement upon IR-induced evaporation as a function or IR frequency from a tunable quantum cascade laser (QCL). We have coined this technique Single Droplet Displacement Infrared Action Spectroscopy (SiDDIRAS). SiDDIRAS does not require complex optics or post-acquisition analyses. This technique is easily reproducible, highly accurate, and, depending on scan speed and needs, can provide up to sub-wavenumber (≤ 1 cm-1) resolution.

In this work, we reported the SiDDIRA spectrum of an ~8 µm droplet containing NaCl and NaN3. Leveraging the sensitivity of the azide anion’s (N3−) asymmetric stretch to the ionic environment, we showed that this droplet remained aqueous while supersaturated with salt through SiDDIRAS and other established methods. The SiDDIRA spectrum confirmed that the N3− anions formed ion pairs with Na+ cations, and that the water hydrogen bonding network of the microdroplet is altered due to the water molecules’ interactions with ions. This work showed the robustness and sensitivity of SiDDIRAS, which will contribute to the arsenal of analytical techniques to unveil many unanswered questions in microdroplet chemistry.

---

## Results

Since the ionic environment of microdroplets is of interest, we chose the N3− anion as a molecular vibrational probe. N3− is a popular vibrational probe because its asymmetric fundamental vibration (νas) in water at 2048 cm-1 (black trace in Figure 1A) does not overlap with other common functional groups such as -OH, -NH, carbonyls, carbonates, and especially water in the mid-IR region. Additionally, νas is sensitive to its environment. Stronger interaction with solvent molecules causes dramatic blueshifts (1987 cm-1 in vacuum31 to 2000 cm-1 in DMSO32 to 2048 cm-1 in water33). Blueshifts are also observed when ion pairs (IPs) are formed. In DMSO, a ~25 cm-1 blueshift is observed when N3− forms contact ion pairs (CIPs) with Na+ cation.32 In aqueous nanoconfined reverse micelles (RMs), a more moderate ~9 cm-1 blueshift for formation of IPs with Na+ ions is observed, presumably due to shielding effect from water-ion interactions.33 The authors in that study assigned the blueshift to formation of IPs in small, nanometer-sized RMs, due to an increase in ion concentration and decrease in water concentration. This phenomenon in nanoconfined water in RMs is known,34, 35, 36, 37, 38, 39, 40 and has been reported to be the reason for the breaking of the hydrogen bonding network,41 which leads to a decrease in proton transfer rate and a shutdown of the Grotthuss mechanism.

We emulated the results from aqueous RMs studies by taking an FTIR spectrum of a saturated NaCl bulk solution at 5.4 M, shown in red in Figure 1A. Indeed, we observed a modest (~4 cm-1) blueshift at 2052 cm-1 in the νas for Na+ ion even at saturation limit at room temperature (Figure 1A). Additionally, the FWHM also increases by ~7 cm-1 as [Na+] increases. This blue shift and peak broadening trend are consistent with previous studies for N3− forming IPs with Na+,32, 33 although those studies did not provide adequate explanations for this broadening behavior. We have previously reported similar line broadening for the nitrile (-CN) group as it forms Lewis bonds with transition metals.42, 43

With the complete knowledge of the spectral behavior of the νas when coupled to Na+, we first isolated a droplet containing NaCl and NaN3 with r = 7.944 µm in the LQ-EDB (see sizing information in Figure 2). The droplet was generated from a bulk solution containing 2.5 g/L (~43 mM) NaCl and 2.5 g/L (~39 mM) NaN3. However, as the droplets are generated in the LQ-EDB, water evaporates, and the composition of the droplet equilibrates with the chamber environment. For that reason, one cannot assume the concentrations in the droplet to be the same as the bulk solution. Determining the concentration of species in microdroplets that are generated in this way will be discussed later. We obtained the SiDDIRA spectrum for the 7.944 µm droplet, with the raw droplet z displacement shown as open black circles in Figure 1B. Details of the data processing are discussed in Section 1.3 in the SI with the raw data shown in Figure S2. The corresponding video of the droplet motion as resonant IR light is turned on and off is also attached. Additionally, for the action spectrum to be meaningful, the droplet displacement must be linear with the laser power, which is discussed in Figure S4. As the droplet displaced upwards, the irradiation efficiency may decrease if the droplet is no longer in the IR laser’s path. The IR beam size in our setup is measured to be ~0.724 mm (details in Section S1.4, Table S2 and Figure S5), which is much bigger than the droplet’s displacement (0.13 mm). Hence, we believe the irradiation efficiency change to be negligible.

The raw droplet displacement data fits well to two Gaussian peaks, shown in red and blue in Figure 1B, which combined to form the black trace in Figure 1B (fitting details discussed in Section S1.3 and the complete fitting parameters shown in Table S1). The red Gaussian centers at 2053 cm-1 with FWHM of 40 cm-1 while the broad blue Gaussian centers at 2101 cm-1 with a FWHM of 80 cm-1. We assigned the red peak as the νas. Compared to FTIR spectra in Figure 2A, the νas from the droplet shows a similar blueshift to the bulk FTIR solution at 5.4 M NaCl but is slightly broader (40 vs. 33 cm-1). Ideally, a calibration between Δz and absorption cross section is desired. However, establishing such a connection in an absolute sense is difficult because of differences in the droplet’s mass-to-charge ratio from experiment to experiment. Nevertheless, this blue shift indicates that the droplet has high ionic content, while the modest increase in spectral width hints at a slight supersaturation, similar to bulk behavior.

The peak at 2101 cm-1 is likely the combination band of the water bend fundamental and the lower frequency libration motions,44, 45, 46 sometimes known as the “association band” (hereafter denoted νcombH2O). Previous bulk FTIR study if this νcombH2O band has shown that it redshifts from ~2135 cm-1 to ~2100 cm-1 as [Na+] increases from 1 to 5 M.46 The reason for this redshift is due to ionic interactions of the ion with the water molecules, which weakens the hydrogen bonding network. The more rigid hydrogen bonding network will thus have a lower average librational frequency, which causes redshift. This feature is often ignored in many studies because of its weak signal. In fact, it can be observed in the bulk FTIR as well if we reduce the NaN3 concentration, which we discuss further in Section S2, Figure S6-S7. The fact that SiDDIRAS can detect the νcombH2O band points to its sensitivity and robustness. Additionally, the νcombH2O redshifting to 2101 cm-1 is further evidence that the droplet has high ionic content.

The deliquescence point for NaCl is at 75%,47, 48 meaning that the droplets will be supersaturated only if the RH in the chamber is below this RH value. To determine the true RH in the chamber and the salt concentrations in the droplets, we applied a dual-droplet hygroscopicity measurement originally developed in our lab.47 First, we measure the RI and radius of the droplet as a function of RH, and the bulk water activity of a high concentration solution. From these measurements, we obtain the radial growth factor (rGF), which can then be used to deduce the salt concentration in the droplets. More details are provided in Section S3 of the SI. To decompose the composition of the multicomponent salt droplet, rGF curves for pure salt and mixed salt droplets were obtained (Figure S8A). Then, using the Zdanovskii-Stokes-Robinson (ZSR) relationship,49 which relates the water content of a mixture to that of the individual solutes at the same water activity, one can estimate the mixed salt content. We assumed an equal mass ratio of the solutes NaCl and NaN3 in the mixture and the predicted rGF is compared against the measured data in Figures S8A, showing excellent agreement. Based on the measured rGF and the approximations described in Section S3, we also estimate the molarity of the solutes in the droplet as a function of RH, shown in Figure S8B. From these measurements, we also obtain the refractive index (RI) as a function of RH, reported for 589 nm in Figure S8C.

To obtain an improved estimate of the in-situ RH during SiDDIRA measurements, we compare the measured RI of the droplet to the dependence reported in Figure S8C. The size and RI of these droplets were determined from the Mie resonance spectra, shown in Figure 2A along with the best-fit simulation. From these data, the RI of the droplet was measured to be 1.384, which corresponds to an RH of ~72% according to Figure S8C. At this RH, [Na+] = 6.1 M and [N3−] = 2.9 M in the droplet, consistent with our earlier interpretation that the SiDDIRA spectrum of NaCl and NaN3, showing that the 5 cm-1 blueshift and peak broadening, is due to supersaturation of salt and formation of IPs.

Other additional factors may contribute to the observed 5 cm-1 blueshift, such as electrostatic field effects from the charged surface or microheterogenous solvation environments at the air-water interface. The electrostatic field effects from the droplet surface are expected to be negligible due to the high salt content of the droplet, resulting in short screening lengths. Furthermore, the majority of the azide ions would have to be aligned with the electric field in order to induce such a large blueshift. Additionally, the charge density on the droplet is quite small. For example, our previous studies of organic azide at the air-water interface showed that a charge density of ~1 e–/nm2 induces a shift in the νasN3 by only 1-2 cm-1.50 Previous measurements of microdroplets trapped in EDBs showed that there are 105 to 106 e– in the droplet.11 Assuming that all of the charge density is at the surface, for a r = 10 µm droplet, the surface charge density will be 10-2 to 10-3 e–/nm2. This surface charge density is several orders of magnitude smaller than the previous study at the air-water interface, and is likely too small to induce measurable shifts. Therefore, we expect the contribution from electrostatic field effects to the blue shift to be negligible. Regarding microheterogenous solvation environments at the air-water interface, we cannot comment on such effect with our current data because this method is not necessarily surface-sensitive. Future studies may use a different vibrational probe that is surface active to deconvolute surface from bulk effects.

To verify that the IR laser does not cause significant evaporation, which could influence [Na+], hence the frequency of the νasN3, we also obtain the Mie spectrum of the NaCl and NaN3 droplet under constant IR illumination at 2053 cm-1, shown in Figure 2B. This measurement shows a ~200 nm change in radius and a small increase in RI. This change in radius corresponds to a ~7.6% reduction in volume at peak absorption, leading to an increase in the concentration from 6.1 M to ~6.5 M. Given the limited sensitivity of the spectrum to [Na+], we do not expect this change to be apparent in our data. Figure 2 indicates that IR absorption by the particle can also be deduced from the change in Mie resonance, as first demonstrated by Arnold et al.28, 29 While this detection method can be more sensitive to small changes in droplet’s response, it is also more laborious, as accurately simulating the Mie spectra require additional post-acquisition analyses. Furthermore, the displacement can cause misalignment of the broadband source for detection of Mie resonances. Hence, we do not see the advantage of using this detection method over monitoring the displacement, which allows the spectral data to be acquired much faster without compromising accuracy.

To get further molecular-level insights on the Na+ −N3− IPs in the droplet, we turn to quantum computational modeling using the Q-Chem program suite at the ωB97M-V/def2-TZVPD level of theory. To verify the robustness of the method, we benchmarked the experimental νasN3 bands obtained in this study against calculated frequencies shown in Table S4. Computational details are discussed further in Section S4. To understand the effect of the hydration shell on the geometry and charge distribution of the IPs, we compared the computational results with and without water, shown in Figure 3.

Figures 3A-B show Na+ −N3− with and without water, respectively. A stark contrast between the gas-phase and hydrated geometries is the Na+ −N1 −N2 bond angle. Without water, this bond angle is 172.9°, which is almost linear, but then bends to 135.2° when hydrated by only six water molecules. Interestingly, the reorientation of the N3− anion geometry as water is added agrees with previous experimental and theoretical gas-phase study by Jungwirth and coworkers51 on microhydrated clusters of N3− ∙(H2O)n. In that study, the authors show that hydrogen bonding from water molecules can stabilize the N3− anion. Their MD simulation also shows that the preferred geometry for the N3− anion is parallel to the water clusters at the vacuum-water interface. In this case, specific hydrogen bond interactions likely cause azide reorientation.

Additionally, charge distribution on Na+ −N3− complex changes significantly upon hydration. We performed natural bond orbital (NBO) analysis for both cases, reported in Tables S6 and S7, respectively. In the bare complex (Table S6), charge distribution is localized between the Na+ −N1 bond with the Na+ carrying most of the positive charge (+0.97) and N1 carrying most of the negative charge (-0.87). The central nitrogen, N2, has some negative character (-0.31) and the terminal nitrogen is slightly positive N3 (0.22). When water molecules are present (Table S7), charges on N1 and N2 are distributed slightly more evenly (-0.62 and -0.51, respectively). This charge redistribution upon hydration can be thought of more clearly in terms of polarizability. Without water, the Na+ cation is much more polarizing to the azide anion and causes electron density to build on N1. Upon hydration, the solvent compensates for this effect and redistributes electron density throughout the complex. In our NBO analysis, we find that charge redistribution, and not Lewis-type interaction, causes the frequency shift.

We have described a new and simple method, called SiDDIRAS, to obtain an IR spectrum of a single micron-size, charged microdroplet. The IR spectrum of an ~8 µm aqueous droplet containing NaCl and NaN3 show significant blue shift of the νasN3. Using this shift in frequency and hygroscopicity measurements, we provided evidence to attribute the spectral shift and broadening from the azide asymmetric stretch to supersaturation of salt and formation of ion pairs in the ~8 µm aqueous droplet. The concentrations of Na+ and N3− were determined to be 6.1 M and 2.9 M, respectively.

Many recent reports have attributed novel behaviors of microdroplets to surface effects such as strong electric fields52 and microsolvation environment at the air-water interface.53 SiDDIRAS is a promising method to investigate these effects. The spectral resolution of this method is limited by the laser, which is 0.1 cm-1 in this case. The signal-to-noise ratio is limited by the detection of the mechanical displacement of the droplet. We note that the spectrum reported in this study is from a single scan at reduced laser power. To detect weaker vibrational modes, one can average multiple scans at higher laser power. Hence, SiDDIRAS is a promising and sensitive technique to uncover some of the unanswered questions in microdroplet chemistry. For example, electrostatic field effects can be probed by changing the droplet’s charge (both magnitude and polarity) and the droplet’s size. The latter requires better control of RH without introducing mechanical displacement of the droplet through humidified gas. Understanding the droplet’s microhetergenous solvation at the surface is also possible by using a surface-active vibrational probe,50 which will require calibrating these probes first on the bulk surface. While this report serves to introduce SiDDIRAS, we foresee performing more quantitative studies as the method matures to clarify some of the unanswered questions in droplet chemistry.

The fact that action spectroscopy is possible for microdroplets by mapping its displacement opens the door for methods and studies that were not possible. For example, droplets that contain UV-Vis chromophore species can be studied using UV-Vis action spectroscopy.54 We suspect that, because UV-Vis chromophores generally have higher absorption cross sections, hence higher energy per absorbed photon (provided there is no fluorescence), the displacement caused by light-induced evaporation might be even more sensitive to UV-Vis absorption. The rich literature of IR spectroscopy on biological systems can now be applied to study in single, substrate-free, levitated microdroplets. Experiments are ongoing to highlight the rich experimental landscape as SiDDIRA continues to mature and evolve.

---

## Methods

The experimental method is discussed in more detail in Section S1 but will be briefly described here. The instrument diagram is shown in Figure 4A with the LQ-EDB inside an environmentally controlled chamber. On either side of the LQ-EDB are the optical setups. On the left, is a broadband LED (620-680 nm, Thorlabs M660L4) focused by a 50 mm biconvex lens which enters the LQ-EDB at an angle through a quartz window. The backscattered light, with the characteristic WGMs, is collected for sizing the droplets (See Figure S1 in Section S1.2 for details on optical setup). On the right is a QCL (MIRcat-QT, Daylight Solutions, 1950-2300 cm-1), which enters the chamber through a CaF2 window. The QCL operates in the continuous wave (CW) mode, scanning in increments of 1 cm-1 with a mechanical shutter attached to a solenoid at its entrance. The solenoid is controlled by a delay generator (SRS DG535), which alternates between allowing the laser to irradiate the droplet for 2 seconds, followed by blocking it for 2 seconds. The cycle repeats for each frequency until the frequency scan is complete. The droplet is illuminated by a 532 nm laser from the bottom of the LQ-EDB. Note that the scattered light from this 532 nm laser is used to illuminate the droplet only and is not collected for optical analysis. A color CMOS camera (Thorlabs CS165CU) mounted in the orthogonal position to the optical paths (not depicted) is used to record the droplet’s position over time as the IR laser scans the frequency range. The recorded centroid position of the droplet is then extracted and processed with a MATLAB code (see Figure S2 in Section 1.3 for details).

Figures 4B-D describe the sequence of events that take place when the IR light interacts with the levitated microdroplet in the LQ-EDB. Initially, when the IR laser is off, the droplet z position is balanced by gravitational pull and the electrical force from the DC electrode (Figure 4B):

mg = qVDC C / z, (1)

where m is the mass of the droplet, g is the gravitational acceleration, q is the droplet’s charge, VDC is the DC voltage on the electrode, z is the distance from the electrode to the droplet, and C is a constant that relates the applied potential on the balancing electrode to the potential felt by the droplet at the equilibrium position. Note that to control the relative humidity (RH), humidified gas is continuously introduced to the chamber, which would add an additional drag force term in Equation 1. However, during IR acquisition, we turn the gas off to prevent this drag force from introducing noise, hence this term is excluded. Additionally, Equation 1 does not account for the inhomogeneity of the electric field as the droplet’s z position increases and is only approximately valid when the droplet is near the balancing electrode. To establish the z distance at which Equation 1 is valid, we performed a measurement of the droplet’s displacement (Δz) as a function of applied voltage (ΔV) on the balancing electrode, shown in Figure S3. Our measurement shows that the droplet’s displacement is linear with the applied voltage up to ~1.5 mm. Because the droplet’s displacement in this study is within this range (vide infra), Equation 1 remains valid.

When the IR laser irradiates the droplet and the frequency is in resonance with IR active absorption features of molecules in the droplet (Figure 4C), the light will be absorbed and converted into heat. This heat will raise the temperature of the droplet, leading to a shift in the water vapor equilibrium and causing water to evaporate from the droplet. The droplet will lose mass and displace upwards:

(m−∆m)g = qVDC C / (z+∆z), (2)

When the laser is turned off, the surrounding moisture condenses back onto the droplet, restoring the droplet to its original position (Figure 4D).

While the radiation pressure and electrostatic coupling between the laser field and the charged droplet can potentially contribute to Δz, we rule out these interactions in our work for the following reasons: 1) Experimental evidence from this work shows that the displacement is in the wrong direction for Δz to be due to the scattering force (which is in the same direction of laser propagation) and the beam is not focused enough to cause a strong gradient force (see Section S1.4, Figure S5). 2) Electrostatic coupling between the laser field and the charged droplet is unlikely because the displacement is composition and excitation frequency dependent. Another concern is whether the droplet remains homogenous during the evaporation/condensation process. Previous studies47, 55 have shown that NaCl microdroplets can remain aqueous until 40% RH before crystallizing, hence we do not foresee the existence of salt crashing out of the droplet, causing inhomogeneity in the solvation environment. Additionally, salt cannot evaporate from the droplet, hence as moisture condenses back onto the droplet after IR irradiation, we expect the salt composition of the droplet to remain the same.

An RH probe (Elitech) was used to ensure the RH reached stable condition but, as mentioned earlier, humidified gas is turned off to eliminate drag force, which interfere with the accuracy of the RH readout. When the humidified gas is turned off, the RH and temperature of the chamber varied by 1-2% and ~0.1°C throughout the IR scan according to the probe. The manufacturer reported the precision of this particular probe to be 3% RH and 0.3°C.To eliminate uncertainty in RH measurements during collection of SiDARRA spectra, we used an in situ dual-droplet technique to infer the RH inside the chamber (vide infra, discussed in more details in Section S3), showing the internal RH to be ~72%. This evaporation/condensation process occurs on the millisecond timescale.56, 57, 58 At each frequency, the droplet interacts with the IR light on the seconds timescale, thus there is enough time for the evaporation/condensation processes to reach steady state. By mapping the displacement of the droplet (∆z) as a function of IR frequency, an IR spectrum of a single charged droplet isolated at ambient conditions in the LQ-EDB can be obtained, illustrated in Figure 4E.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

Single Droplet Displacement Infrared Action Spectroscopy
The authors present a new method of measuring the chemical environment inside individual water droplets. The procedure
allows access to a previously poorly understood but important environment, and combines standard tools in a novel and
clever way. The research is understandable and approachable.
The paper is clearly written and convincingly argues that the authors did what they say. The writing is clear, albeit a little
verbose.
A few aspects of the technique could be explained more clearly. One example is the imaging system. The reader is
challenged to understand exactly what light is collected where. In particular, figure 1A contains no imaging optics;
presumably both scattered 532 nm light and scattered LED light (?) are collected, but this is not clear. Obviously this
description can be corrected.
Most readers of the paper (including myself!) are not experts in droplet chemistry. It would be helpful if a summary of the
droplet were included. How many N3- ions are in this small, but macroscopic, droplet?
The technique is innovative, convincingly demonstrated, and potentially transformative in the somewhat niche field of droplet
chemistry. In addition, the technique appears to be tractable enough that it will be reproducible by other groups.
The authors make a considerable effort to propose extensions of the technique. This is the crux of acceptance to Nature
Communications. My own judgement, from outside the field, is that there is. I am far from an expert in this field, but this is
relevant to electrospray ionization (certainly a widely used tool), as well as atmospheric chemistry, where water droplets are
of course very relevant. There is a small but non-zero chance to become a widely used technique, of which this would be the
seminal paper.
The paper is unusual, and innovative. It is the type of paper I believe broadens the scientific conversation, and leads to new
scientific ideas. As such, I support its publication in nature communications.

### Reviewer 2

Comments:
This paper presents a novel method for observing the IR spectrum of a single droplet levitated in an electrodynamic trap.
The IR spectrum is measured by the displacement of the trapped droplet due to evaporation and mass loss induced by the
absorption of IR light by the droplet. This paper is well-written and provides a novel methodology to measure the IR
spectrum of a single droplet. Therefore, this paper is considered worthy of publication. However, the following points are
required to be considered before publication.
1. Some papers have reported spectral measurements of a single particle in the electrodynamic trap. [1,2] The author should
properly cite these papers and clearly state the differences from the previous reports.
[1] S. Arnold, M. Neuman, A. B. Pluchino, “Molecular spectroscopy of a single aerosol particle.” Opt. Lett. 1984, 9, 4–6.
[2] S. Arnold, E. K. Murphy, G. Sageev, “Aerosol particle molecular spectroscopy” Appl. Opt. 1985, 24, 1048.
2. Photophoretic force on a single particle in the electrodynamic trap has been measured by the displacement of the particle
in the trap. [3,4] The author should properly cite these papers and state that they applied similar phenomena to spectral
measurements.
[3] H.-B. Lin, “Infrared absorption spectroscopy of single particles using photophoresis” Opt. Lett. 1985, 10, 68.
[4] O. Krauß, G. Wurm, “Radiation pressure forces on individual micron-size dust particles: A new experimental approach” J.
Quant. Spectrosc. Radiat. Transf. 2004, 89, 179–189.
3. Equation (1) assumes that the electric field is identical from the bottom to the top of the linear trap. However, the electric
field is not homogeneous with respect to z due to the disturbance caused by the linear electrodes. Equation (1) is only
approximately valid in the vicinity of the trapped particle.
4. Figure S3 shows that the displacement of the particle reaches 0.13 mm. The authors should specify the beam size of the
IR laser, because the irradiation efficiency may decrease due to the particle displacement.
5. Figure 3 indicates that the IR absorption by the particle can also be detected from the spectral shifts of the Mie spectra.
Discussion on the applicability of the spectral shift will help the understanding of the advantage of the present method.
6. Chemical formulas (N3-, Na+, etc) should be written in upright type.

### Reviewer 3

In this study, Prof. Dawalty and Coworkers report a novel approach, termed Single Droplet Displacement Infrared Action Spectroscopy (SiDDIRAS), which enables acquisition of IR spectra from single, levitated microdroplets confined within a linear quadrupole electrodynamic balance (LQ-EDB). By tracking the droplet’s displacement as a function of IR frequency, they convert mass-loss-driven motion into an “action spectrum.” The study represents an exciting methodological advance, addressing a long-standing challenge in probing the molecular environments of individual microdroplet systems central to both analytical and atmospheric chemistry. The work is technically sophisticated and conceptually impactful; however, several key aspects require clarification and control to ensure robustness of these techniques. On this, I have several queries and suggestions, which are outlined below.
1. The central claim of the work, that IR absorption induces droplet motion through resonant heating and evaporation,
requires more stringent control. Could radiation pressure or electrostatic coupling between the laser field and the charged
droplet also contribute to Δz? Quantitative analysis or modeling of the force balance would strengthen confidence in the
interpretation. The author should address this.
2. Is there a calibration curve linking Δz to a known absorption cross-section or optical density, perhaps using droplets of
other composition (e.g., D2O)? Without such calibration, the technique risks being limited to qualitative shifts rather than
quantitative intensity analysis. Authors are suggested to clarify this.

droplet remains aqueous, hence the ions are under a homogenous solvation

## Paper

## Abstract

Aqueous microdroplets have fascinated scientists with unique properties that deviate from bulk solutions. Understanding microdroplet chemistry has been limited by few spectroscopic measurements on single well-defined microdroplets. Here we present a new technique to record an IR spectrum of a single droplet called Single Droplet Displacement Infrared Action Spectroscopy (SiDDIRAS) with potential broad applications in physical, analytical, and environmental chemistry. The droplet was trapped in a linear quadrupole electrodynamic balance. When IR radiation at resonant frequency was introduced, mass loss from IR-induced evaporation caused the droplet to displace upwards. Mapping the displacement as a function of IR frequency yields an IR spectrum of a single microdroplet. As a demonstration, the SiDDIRA spectrum of an ~8 µm droplet containing NaCl and NaN3 shows that the azide asymmetric stretch blueshifts by 5 cm-1 relative to bulk with significant peak broadening, evidence that this droplet is supersaturated with salts compared to bulk solutions.

---

## Introduction

Electrospray ionization (ESI) remains a popular method to introduce ions and charged biomolecules to a mass spectrometer for analysis since its invention in the 1960s.1 Yet the complex ionization process from charged droplets to charged ions continues to be a topic of active research.2, 3 More recently, using ESI and pneumatic sprays, studies by several groups have reported enhanced chemical reactivity in microdroplets.4, 5, 6, 7, 8 More broadly, chemistry occurring in droplets and aerosol particles in the environment has great impact on atmospheric chemistry and climate.9

The electrodynamic balance is a class of instruments that have been used to study microdroplets for decades. In recent years, the linear quadrupole electrodynamic balance (LQ-EDB) has become popular.10 The LQ-EDB laterally confines charged droplets by applying AC voltages to four cylindrical rods held in a quadrupole configuration (Figure 4A, vide infra) while balancing gravity on the droplet with a DC voltage (Figure 4B, vide infra). The LQ-EDB is held in an environmentally controlled chamber and can be coupled with various optical techniques to obtain physical information such as radius,11 refractive index (RI),12 hygroscopicity,13 and viscosity.14 Specifically, in our set up, a broadband LED is used to collect back-scattered light with characteristic whispering gallery modes (WGMs) from the droplet to determine its radius and RI simultaneously (left in Figure 4A, vide in fra), as described previously12 and in more detail in Section S1.2 in the Supporting Information (SI). The chemical composition of the droplet can also be obtained by coupling the LQ-EDB with Raman13, 15 or fluorescence16 spectroscopies and mass spectrometry,17, 18, 19 further highlighting the versatility of the instrument.

Among these techniques, the use of IR spectroscopy for measuring single droplets has been limited, despite its potential for revealing the unique chemical microenvironment of the droplets, especially its sensitivity to changes in the hydrogen bonding network of water. Traditional FTIR measurements are not possible with trapped micron-sized droplets due to scattering and the small optical path length. IR spectroscopy studies based on optical photothermal effects have been reported for droplets deposited on a substrate,20, 21, 22 but the droplet-substrate interface might interfere with droplet chemistry. Additionally, the charge state and radius of such droplet is difficult to determine. To overcome these challenges, we report a new type of IR “action” spectroscopy, the principle of which has provided, and continues to provide, deep chemical and physical insights in the gas-phase community for the past few decades.23, 24, 25, 26, 27

Action IR spectroscopy on aerosol particles trapped in an EDB were first introduced by several groups in the 1980s. Arnold et al.28, 29 described a technique called Structure Resonance Molecular Spectroscopy (SRMS), where the authors induced an ammonium sulfate droplet’s evaporation at a certain IR frequency using an SiC Glo-Bar. The fractional change in a droplet’s scattering pattern upon resonant IR-induced evaporation is then fitted with Mie theory and mapped as a function of IR frequency to produce an IR spectrum. Lin30 followed with a method for measuring an action IR spectrum of solid particles, where the photophoretic force acting on a trapped solid ammonium sulfate particle upon absorbing IR photons from a CO laser displaced the particle from its original position. Thus, by measuring the fractional change in balancing voltage required to bring the particle back to its original position (ΔV/V) and mapping it to the IR frequency, an action spectrum was obtained.

Based on these seminal works, we described below an action IR technique for aqueous microdroplets in a LQ-EDB that does not require complex Mie fittings, as shown in Arnold et al.’s works.28, 29 In a way, our detection method is more similar to that described by Lin30 in that we are using the droplet’s displacement from its original position in our measurement. However, we want to stress that we are not measuring the photophoretic force acting on the droplet nor the fractional voltage to bring the droplet back to its original position. Instead, we are mapping the magnitude of the droplet’s displacement upon IR-induced evaporation as a function or IR frequency from a tunable quantum cascade laser (QCL). We have coined this technique Single Droplet Displacement Infrared Action Spectroscopy (SiDDIRAS). SiDDIRAS does not require complex optics or post-acquisition analyses. This technique is easily reproducible, highly accurate, and, depending on scan speed and needs, can provide up to sub-wavenumber (≤ 1 cm-1) resolution.

In this work, we reported the SiDDIRA spectrum of an ~8 µm droplet containing NaCl and NaN3. Leveraging the sensitivity of the azide anion’s (N3−) asymmetric stretch to the ionic environment, we showed that this droplet remained aqueous while supersaturated with salt through SiDDIRAS and other established methods. The SiDDIRA spectrum confirmed that the N3− anions formed ion pairs with Na+ cations, and that the water hydrogen bonding network of the microdroplet is altered due to the water molecules’ interactions with ions. This work showed the robustness and sensitivity of SiDDIRAS, which will contribute to the arsenal of analytical techniques to unveil many unanswered questions in microdroplet chemistry.

---

## Results

Since the ionic environment of microdroplets is of interest, we chose the N3− anion as a molecular vibrational probe. N3− is a popular vibrational probe because its asymmetric fundamental vibration (νas) in water at 2048 cm-1 (black trace in Figure 1A) does not overlap with other common functional groups such as -OH, -NH, carbonyls, carbonates, and especially water in the mid-IR region. Additionally, νas is sensitive to its environment. Stronger interaction with solvent molecules causes dramatic blueshifts (1987 cm-1 in vacuum31 to 2000 cm-1 in DMSO32 to 2048 cm-1 in water33). Blueshifts are also observed when ion pairs (IPs) are formed. In DMSO, a ~25 cm-1 blueshift is observed when N3− forms contact ion pairs (CIPs) with Na+ cation.32 In aqueous nanoconfined reverse micelles (RMs), a more moderate ~9 cm-1 blueshift for formation of IPs with Na+ ions is observed, presumably due to shielding effect from water-ion interactions.33 The authors in that study assigned the blueshift to formation of IPs in small, nanometer-sized RMs, due to an increase in ion concentration and decrease in water concentration. This phenomenon in nanoconfined water in RMs is known,34, 35, 36, 37, 38, 39, 40 and has been reported to be the reason for the breaking of the hydrogen bonding network,41 which leads to a decrease in proton transfer rate and a shutdown of the Grotthuss mechanism.

We emulated the results from aqueous RMs studies by taking an FTIR spectrum of a saturated NaCl bulk solution at 5.4 M, shown in red in Figure 1A. Indeed, we observed a modest (~4 cm-1) blueshift at 2052 cm-1 in the νas for Na+ ion even at saturation limit at room temperature (Figure 1A). Additionally, the FWHM also increases by ~7 cm-1 as [Na+] increases. This blue shift and peak broadening trend are consistent with previous studies for N3− forming IPs with Na+,32, 33 although those studies did not provide adequate explanations for this broadening behavior. We have previously reported similar line broadening for the nitrile (-CN) group as it forms Lewis bonds with transition metals.42, 43

With the complete knowledge of the spectral behavior of the νas when coupled to Na+, we first isolated a droplet containing NaCl and NaN3 with r = 7.944 µm in the LQ-EDB (see sizing information in Figure 2). The droplet was generated from a bulk solution containing 2.5 g/L (~43 mM) NaCl and 2.5 g/L (~39 mM) NaN3. However, as the droplets are generated in the LQ-EDB, water evaporates, and the composition of the droplet equilibrates with the chamber environment. For that reason, one cannot assume the concentrations in the droplet to be the same as the bulk solution. Determining the concentration of species in microdroplets that are generated in this way will be discussed later. We obtained the SiDDIRA spectrum for the 7.944 µm droplet, with the raw droplet z displacement shown as open black circles in Figure 1B. Details of the data processing are discussed in Section 1.3 in the SI with the raw data shown in Figure S2. The corresponding video of the droplet motion as resonant IR light is turned on and off is also attached. Additionally, for the action spectrum to be meaningful, the droplet displacement must be linear with the laser power, which is discussed in Figure S4. As the droplet displaced upwards, the irradiation efficiency may decrease if the droplet is no longer in the IR laser’s path. The IR beam size in our setup is measured to be ~0.724 mm (details in Section S1.4, Table S2 and Figure S5), which is much bigger than the droplet’s displacement (0.13 mm). Hence, we believe the irradiation efficiency change to be negligible.

The raw droplet displacement data fits well to two Gaussian peaks, shown in red and blue in Figure 1B, which combined to form the black trace in Figure 1B (fitting details discussed in Section S1.3 and the complete fitting parameters shown in Table S1). The red Gaussian centers at 2053 cm-1 with FWHM of 40 cm-1 while the broad blue Gaussian centers at 2101 cm-1 with a FWHM of 80 cm-1. We assigned the red peak as the νas. Compared to FTIR spectra in Figure 2A, the νas from the droplet shows a similar blueshift to the bulk FTIR solution at 5.4 M NaCl but is slightly broader (40 vs. 33 cm-1). Ideally, a calibration between Δz and absorption cross section is desired. However, establishing such a connection in an absolute sense is difficult because of differences in the droplet’s mass-to-charge ratio from experiment to experiment. Nevertheless, this blue shift indicates that the droplet has high ionic content, while the modest increase in spectral width hints at a slight supersaturation, similar to bulk behavior.

The peak at 2101 cm-1 is likely the combination band of the water bend fundamental and the lower frequency libration motions,44, 45, 46 sometimes known as the “association band” (hereafter denoted νcombH2O). Previous bulk FTIR study if this νcombH2O band has shown that it redshifts from ~2135 cm-1 to ~2100 cm-1 as [Na+] increases from 1 to 5 M.46 The reason for this redshift is due to ionic interactions of the ion with the water molecules, which weakens the hydrogen bonding network. The more rigid hydrogen bonding network will thus have a lower average librational frequency, which causes redshift. This feature is often ignored in many studies because of its weak signal. In fact, it can be observed in the bulk FTIR as well if we reduce the NaN3 concentration, which we discuss further in Section S2, Figure S6-S7. The fact that SiDDIRAS can detect the νcombH2O band points to its sensitivity and robustness. Additionally, the νcombH2O redshifting to 2101 cm-1 is further evidence that the droplet has high ionic content.

The deliquescence point for NaCl is at 75%,47, 48 meaning that the droplets will be supersaturated only if the RH in the chamber is below this RH value. To determine the true RH in the chamber and the salt concentrations in the droplets, we applied a dual-droplet hygroscopicity measurement originally developed in our lab.47 First, we measure the RI and radius of the droplet as a function of RH, and the bulk water activity of a high concentration solution. From these measurements, we obtain the radial growth factor (rGF), which can then be used to deduce the salt concentration in the droplets. More details are provided in Section S3 of the SI. To decompose the composition of the multicomponent salt droplet, rGF curves for pure salt and mixed salt droplets were obtained (Figure S8A). Then, using the Zdanovskii-Stokes-Robinson (ZSR) relationship,49 which relates the water content of a mixture to that of the individual solutes at the same water activity, one can estimate the mixed salt content. We assumed an equal mass ratio of the solutes NaCl and NaN3 in the mixture and the predicted rGF is compared against the measured data in Figures S8A, showing excellent agreement. Based on the measured rGF and the approximations described in Section S3, we also estimate the molarity of the solutes in the droplet as a function of RH, shown in Figure S8B. From these measurements, we also obtain the refractive index (RI) as a function of RH, reported for 589 nm in Figure S8C.

To obtain an improved estimate of the in-situ RH during SiDDIRA measurements, we compare the measured RI of the droplet to the dependence reported in Figure S8C. The size and RI of these droplets were determined from the Mie resonance spectra, shown in Figure 2A along with the best-fit simulation. From these data, the RI of the droplet was measured to be 1.384, which corresponds to an RH of ~72% according to Figure S8C. At this RH, [Na+] = 6.1 M and [N3−] = 2.9 M in the droplet, consistent with our earlier interpretation that the SiDDIRA spectrum of NaCl and NaN3, showing that the 5 cm-1 blueshift and peak broadening, is due to supersaturation of salt and formation of IPs.

Other additional factors may contribute to the observed 5 cm-1 blueshift, such as electrostatic field effects from the charged surface or microheterogenous solvation environments at the air-water interface. The electrostatic field effects from the droplet surface are expected to be negligible due to the high salt content of the droplet, resulting in short screening lengths. Furthermore, the majority of the azide ions would have to be aligned with the electric field in order to induce such a large blueshift. Additionally, the charge density on the droplet is quite small. For example, our previous studies of organic azide at the air-water interface showed that a charge density of ~1 e–/nm2 induces a shift in the νasN3 by only 1-2 cm-1.50 Previous measurements of microdroplets trapped in EDBs showed that there are 105 to 106 e– in the droplet.11 Assuming that all of the charge density is at the surface, for a r = 10 µm droplet, the surface charge density will be 10-2 to 10-3 e–/nm2. This surface charge density is several orders of magnitude smaller than the previous study at the air-water interface, and is likely too small to induce measurable shifts. Therefore, we expect the contribution from electrostatic field effects to the blue shift to be negligible. Regarding microheterogenous solvation environments at the air-water interface, we cannot comment on such effect with our current data because this method is not necessarily surface-sensitive. Future studies may use a different vibrational probe that is surface active to deconvolute surface from bulk effects.

To verify that the IR laser does not cause significant evaporation, which could influence [Na+], hence the frequency of the νasN3, we also obtain the Mie spectrum of the NaCl and NaN3 droplet under constant IR illumination at 2053 cm-1, shown in Figure 2B. This measurement shows a ~200 nm change in radius and a small increase in RI. This change in radius corresponds to a ~7.6% reduction in volume at peak absorption, leading to an increase in the concentration from 6.1 M to ~6.5 M. Given the limited sensitivity of the spectrum to [Na+], we do not expect this change to be apparent in our data. Figure 2 indicates that IR absorption by the particle can also be deduced from the change in Mie resonance, as first demonstrated by Arnold et al.28, 29 While this detection method can be more sensitive to small changes in droplet’s response, it is also more laborious, as accurately simulating the Mie spectra require additional post-acquisition analyses. Furthermore, the displacement can cause misalignment of the broadband source for detection of Mie resonances. Hence, we do not see the advantage of using this detection method over monitoring the displacement, which allows the spectral data to be acquired much faster without compromising accuracy.

To get further molecular-level insights on the Na+ −N3− IPs in the droplet, we turn to quantum computational modeling using the Q-Chem program suite at the ωB97M-V/def2-TZVPD level of theory. To verify the robustness of the method, we benchmarked the experimental νasN3 bands obtained in this study against calculated frequencies shown in Table S4. Computational details are discussed further in Section S4. To understand the effect of the hydration shell on the geometry and charge distribution of the IPs, we compared the computational results with and without water, shown in Figure 3.

Figures 3A-B show Na+ −N3− with and without water, respectively. A stark contrast between the gas-phase and hydrated geometries is the Na+ −N1 −N2 bond angle. Without water, this bond angle is 172.9°, which is almost linear, but then bends to 135.2° when hydrated by only six water molecules. Interestingly, the reorientation of the N3− anion geometry as water is added agrees with previous experimental and theoretical gas-phase study by Jungwirth and coworkers51 on microhydrated clusters of N3− ∙(H2O)n. In that study, the authors show that hydrogen bonding from water molecules can stabilize the N3− anion. Their MD simulation also shows that the preferred geometry for the N3− anion is parallel to the water clusters at the vacuum-water interface. In this case, specific hydrogen bond interactions likely cause azide reorientation.

Additionally, charge distribution on Na+ −N3− complex changes significantly upon hydration. We performed natural bond orbital (NBO) analysis for both cases, reported in Tables S6 and S7, respectively. In the bare complex (Table S6), charge distribution is localized between the Na+ −N1 bond with the Na+ carrying most of the positive charge (+0.97) and N1 carrying most of the negative charge (-0.87). The central nitrogen, N2, has some negative character (-0.31) and the terminal nitrogen is slightly positive N3 (0.22). When water molecules are present (Table S7), charges on N1 and N2 are distributed slightly more evenly (-0.62 and -0.51, respectively). This charge redistribution upon hydration can be thought of more clearly in terms of polarizability. Without water, the Na+ cation is much more polarizing to the azide anion and causes electron density to build on N1. Upon hydration, the solvent compensates for this effect and redistributes electron density throughout the complex. In our NBO analysis, we find that charge redistribution, and not Lewis-type interaction, causes the frequency shift.

We have described a new and simple method, called SiDDIRAS, to obtain an IR spectrum of a single micron-size, charged microdroplet. The IR spectrum of an ~8 µm aqueous droplet containing NaCl and NaN3 show significant blue shift of the νasN3. Using this shift in frequency and hygroscopicity measurements, we provided evidence to attribute the spectral shift and broadening from the azide asymmetric stretch to supersaturation of salt and formation of ion pairs in the ~8 µm aqueous droplet. The concentrations of Na+ and N3− were determined to be 6.1 M and 2.9 M, respectively.

Many recent reports have attributed novel behaviors of microdroplets to surface effects such as strong electric fields52 and microsolvation environment at the air-water interface.53 SiDDIRAS is a promising method to investigate these effects. The spectral resolution of this method is limited by the laser, which is 0.1 cm-1 in this case. The signal-to-noise ratio is limited by the detection of the mechanical displacement of the droplet. We note that the spectrum reported in this study is from a single scan at reduced laser power. To detect weaker vibrational modes, one can average multiple scans at higher laser power. Hence, SiDDIRAS is a promising and sensitive technique to uncover some of the unanswered questions in microdroplet chemistry. For example, electrostatic field effects can be probed by changing the droplet’s charge (both magnitude and polarity) and the droplet’s size. The latter requires better control of RH without introducing mechanical displacement of the droplet through humidified gas. Understanding the droplet’s microhetergenous solvation at the surface is also possible by using a surface-active vibrational probe,50 which will require calibrating these probes first on the bulk surface. While this report serves to introduce SiDDIRAS, we foresee performing more quantitative studies as the method matures to clarify some of the unanswered questions in droplet chemistry.

The fact that action spectroscopy is possible for microdroplets by mapping its displacement opens the door for methods and studies that were not possible. For example, droplets that contain UV-Vis chromophore species can be studied using UV-Vis action spectroscopy.54 We suspect that, because UV-Vis chromophores generally have higher absorption cross sections, hence higher energy per absorbed photon (provided there is no fluorescence), the displacement caused by light-induced evaporation might be even more sensitive to UV-Vis absorption. The rich literature of IR spectroscopy on biological systems can now be applied to study in single, substrate-free, levitated microdroplets. Experiments are ongoing to highlight the rich experimental landscape as SiDDIRA continues to mature and evolve.

---

## Methods

The experimental method is discussed in more detail in Section S1 but will be briefly described here. The instrument diagram is shown in Figure 4A with the LQ-EDB inside an environmentally controlled chamber. On either side of the LQ-EDB are the optical setups. On the left, is a broadband LED (620-680 nm, Thorlabs M660L4) focused by a 50 mm biconvex lens which enters the LQ-EDB at an angle through a quartz window. The backscattered light, with the characteristic WGMs, is collected for sizing the droplets (See Figure S1 in Section S1.2 for details on optical setup). On the right is a QCL (MIRcat-QT, Daylight Solutions, 1950-2300 cm-1), which enters the chamber through a CaF2 window. The QCL operates in the continuous wave (CW) mode, scanning in increments of 1 cm-1 with a mechanical shutter attached to a solenoid at its entrance. The solenoid is controlled by a delay generator (SRS DG535), which alternates between allowing the laser to irradiate the droplet for 2 seconds, followed by blocking it for 2 seconds. The cycle repeats for each frequency until the frequency scan is complete. The droplet is illuminated by a 532 nm laser from the bottom of the LQ-EDB. Note that the scattered light from this 532 nm laser is used to illuminate the droplet only and is not collected for optical analysis. A color CMOS camera (Thorlabs CS165CU) mounted in the orthogonal position to the optical paths (not depicted) is used to record the droplet’s position over time as the IR laser scans the frequency range. The recorded centroid position of the droplet is then extracted and processed with a MATLAB code (see Figure S2 in Section 1.3 for details).

Figures 4B-D describe the sequence of events that take place when the IR light interacts with the levitated microdroplet in the LQ-EDB. Initially, when the IR laser is off, the droplet z position is balanced by gravitational pull and the electrical force from the DC electrode (Figure 4B):

mg = qVDC C / z, (1)

where m is the mass of the droplet, g is the gravitational acceleration, q is the droplet’s charge, VDC is the DC voltage on the electrode, z is the distance from the electrode to the droplet, and C is a constant that relates the applied potential on the balancing electrode to the potential felt by the droplet at the equilibrium position. Note that to control the relative humidity (RH), humidified gas is continuously introduced to the chamber, which would add an additional drag force term in Equation 1. However, during IR acquisition, we turn the gas off to prevent this drag force from introducing noise, hence this term is excluded. Additionally, Equation 1 does not account for the inhomogeneity of the electric field as the droplet’s z position increases and is only approximately valid when the droplet is near the balancing electrode. To establish the z distance at which Equation 1 is valid, we performed a measurement of the droplet’s displacement (Δz) as a function of applied voltage (ΔV) on the balancing electrode, shown in Figure S3. Our measurement shows that the droplet’s displacement is linear with the applied voltage up to ~1.5 mm. Because the droplet’s displacement in this study is within this range (vide infra), Equation 1 remains valid.

When the IR laser irradiates the droplet and the frequency is in resonance with IR active absorption features of molecules in the droplet (Figure 4C), the light will be absorbed and converted into heat. This heat will raise the temperature of the droplet, leading to a shift in the water vapor equilibrium and causing water to evaporate from the droplet. The droplet will lose mass and displace upwards:

(m−∆m)g = qVDC C / (z+∆z), (2)

When the laser is turned off, the surrounding moisture condenses back onto the droplet, restoring the droplet to its original position (Figure 4D).

While the radiation pressure and electrostatic coupling between the laser field and the charged droplet can potentially contribute to Δz, we rule out these interactions in our work for the following reasons: 1) Experimental evidence from this work shows that the displacement is in the wrong direction for Δz to be due to the scattering force (which is in the same direction of laser propagation) and the beam is not focused enough to cause a strong gradient force (see Section S1.4, Figure S5). 2) Electrostatic coupling between the laser field and the charged droplet is unlikely because the displacement is composition and excitation frequency dependent. Another concern is whether the droplet remains homogenous during the evaporation/condensation process. Previous studies47, 55 have shown that NaCl microdroplets can remain aqueous until 40% RH before crystallizing, hence we do not foresee the existence of salt crashing out of the droplet, causing inhomogeneity in the solvation environment. Additionally, salt cannot evaporate from the droplet, hence as moisture condenses back onto the droplet after IR irradiation, we expect the salt composition of the droplet to remain the same.

An RH probe (Elitech) was used to ensure the RH reached stable condition but, as mentioned earlier, humidified gas is turned off to eliminate drag force, which interfere with the accuracy of the RH readout. When the humidified gas is turned off, the RH and temperature of the chamber varied by 1-2% and ~0.1°C throughout the IR scan according to the probe. The manufacturer reported the precision of this particular probe to be 3% RH and 0.3°C.To eliminate uncertainty in RH measurements during collection of SiDARRA spectra, we used an in situ dual-droplet technique to infer the RH inside the chamber (vide infra, discussed in more details in Section S3), showing the internal RH to be ~72%. This evaporation/condensation process occurs on the millisecond timescale.56, 57, 58 At each frequency, the droplet interacts with the IR light on the seconds timescale, thus there is enough time for the evaporation/condensation processes to reach steady state. By mapping the displacement of the droplet (∆z) as a function of IR frequency, an IR spectrum of a single charged droplet isolated at ambient conditions in the LQ-EDB can be obtained, illustrated in Figure 4E.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

Single Droplet Displacement Infrared Action Spectroscopy
The authors present a new method of measuring the chemical environment inside individual water droplets. The procedure
allows access to a previously poorly understood but important environment, and combines standard tools in a novel and
clever way. The research is understandable and approachable.
The paper is clearly written and convincingly argues that the authors did what they say. The writing is clear, albeit a little
verbose.
A few aspects of the technique could be explained more clearly. One example is the imaging system. The reader is
challenged to understand exactly what light is collected where. In particular, figure 1A contains no imaging optics;
presumably both scattered 532 nm light and scattered LED light (?) are collected, but this is not clear. Obviously this
description can be corrected.
Most readers of the paper (including myself!) are not experts in droplet chemistry. It would be helpful if a summary of the
droplet were included. How many N3- ions are in this small, but macroscopic, droplet?
The technique is innovative, convincingly demonstrated, and potentially transformative in the somewhat niche field of droplet
chemistry. In addition, the technique appears to be tractable enough that it will be reproducible by other groups.
The authors make a considerable effort to propose extensions of the technique. This is the crux of acceptance to Nature
Communications. My own judgement, from outside the field, is that there is. I am far from an expert in this field, but this is
relevant to electrospray ionization (certainly a widely used tool), as well as atmospheric chemistry, where water droplets are
of course very relevant. There is a small but non-zero chance to become a widely used technique, of which this would be the
seminal paper.
The paper is unusual, and innovative. It is the type of paper I believe broadens the scientific conversation, and leads to new
scientific ideas. As such, I support its publication in nature communications.

### Reviewer 2

Comments:
This paper presents a novel method for observing the IR spectrum of a single droplet levitated in an electrodynamic trap.
The IR spectrum is measured by the displacement of the trapped droplet due to evaporation and mass loss induced by the
absorption of IR light by the droplet. This paper is well-written and provides a novel methodology to measure the IR
spectrum of a single droplet. Therefore, this paper is considered worthy of publication. However, the following points are
required to be considered before publication.
1. Some papers have reported spectral measurements of a single particle in the electrodynamic trap. [1,2] The author should
properly cite these papers and clearly state the differences from the previous reports.
[1] S. Arnold, M. Neuman, A. B. Pluchino, “Molecular spectroscopy of a single aerosol particle.” Opt. Lett. 1984, 9, 4–6.
[2] S. Arnold, E. K. Murphy, G. Sageev, “Aerosol particle molecular spectroscopy” Appl. Opt. 1985, 24, 1048.
2. Photophoretic force on a single particle in the electrodynamic trap has been measured by the displacement of the particle
in the trap. [3,4] The author should properly cite these papers and state that they applied similar phenomena to spectral
measurements.
[3] H.-B. Lin, “Infrared absorption spectroscopy of single particles using photophoresis” Opt. Lett. 1985, 10, 68.
[4] O. Krauß, G. Wurm, “Radiation pressure forces on individual micron-size dust particles: A new experimental approach” J.
Quant. Spectrosc. Radiat. Transf. 2004, 89, 179–189.
3. Equation (1) assumes that the electric field is identical from the bottom to the top of the linear trap. However, the electric
field is not homogeneous with respect to z due to the disturbance caused by the linear electrodes. Equation (1) is only
approximately valid in the vicinity of the trapped particle.
4. Figure S3 shows that the displacement of the particle reaches 0.13 mm. The authors should specify the beam size of the
IR laser, because the irradiation efficiency may decrease due to the particle displacement.
5. Figure 3 indicates that the IR absorption by the particle can also be detected from the spectral shifts of the Mie spectra.
Discussion on the applicability of the spectral shift will help the understanding of the advantage of the present method.
6. Chemical formulas (N3-, Na+, etc) should be written in upright type.

### Reviewer 3

In this study, Prof. Dawalty and Coworkers report a novel approach, termed Single Droplet Displacement Infrared Action Spectroscopy (SiDDIRAS), which enables acquisition of IR spectra from single, levitated microdroplets confined within a linear quadrupole electrodynamic balance (LQ-EDB). By tracking the droplet’s displacement as a function of IR frequency, they convert mass-loss-driven motion into an “action spectrum.” The study represents an exciting methodological advance, addressing a long-standing challenge in probing the molecular environments of individual microdroplet systems central to both analytical and atmospheric chemistry. The work is technically sophisticated and conceptually impactful; however, several key aspects require clarification and control to ensure robustness of these techniques. On this, I have several queries and suggestions, which are outlined below.
1. The central claim of the work, that IR absorption induces droplet motion through resonant heating and evaporation,
requires more stringent control. Could radiation pressure or electrostatic coupling between the laser field and the charged
droplet also contribute to Δz? Quantitative analysis or modeling of the force balance would strengthen confidence in the
interpretation. The author should address this.
2. Is there a calibration curve linking Δz to a known absorption cross-section or optical density, perhaps using droplets of
other composition (e.g., D2O)? Without such calibration, the technique risks being limited to qualitative shifts rather than
quantitative intensity analysis. Authors are suggested to clarify this.
3. What are the error margins in droplet radius, RI, and the ZSR-based solute estimation?
4. Please comment on whether the droplets were homogeneous throughout the optical measurement period.
5. The observed 5 cm⁻¹ blueshift and significant broadening of ν(N₃⁻) are attributed to Na⁺–N₃⁻ ion-pairing and
supersaturation, but additional factors may contribute. Could electrostatic field effects from the charged droplet surface or
microheterogeneous solvation play roles? Please comment.

Action IR spectroscopy on aerosol particles trapped in an EDB were first introduced by several
groups in the 1980s. Arnold et al.28,29 described a technique called Structure Resonance Molecular
Spectroscopy (SRMS), where the authors induced an ammonium sulfate droplet’s evaporation at
a certain IR frequency using an SiC Glo-Bar. The fractional change in a droplet’s scattering pattern

2

complex optics or post-acquisition analyses. This technique is easily reproducible, highly
accurate, and, depending on scan speed and needs, can provide up to sub-wavenumber (≤ 1 cm-1)

The uncertainty in the radius is typically less than ±5nm (around 0.1%), and this arises from the precision
to which the peak positions are measured. The uncertainty in the RI is less than ±0.005, with measurements
usually closer to ±0.001.
The uncertainty in that size propagates to the uncertainty in the solute concentration estimates, via the radial
growth factor (rGF), although the exact uncertainty depends on the specifics of the measurement.
In general, the uncertainty in the rGF is the error additive sum of the uncertainty in the radius and the
uncertainty in the dry size. The uncertainty in the latter comes from the accuracy of the bulk solution
concentration measurement, which we estimate to be better than ±0.1% based on mass balance precision
and volumetric flask precision, the accuracy of the bulk water activity measurement, which is ~0.3%, and
the accuracy of the water activity measured in the LQ-EDB using the dual-droplet approach, on the order
of ~0.1%. In our method, the droplet radius at a water activity equal to the bulk water activity is used to
determine the dry size. The uncertainty in the water activity meter dominates the uncertainty in this process,
leading to approximately 0.5% uncertainty in the droplet size at the bulk activity measurement water
activity. Thus, the dry size has an error of approximately the same size. The error in the rGF is thus 0.6%
which corresponds to an error in the molarity of 1.8%.

Author Response: We interpret the reviewer’s question regarding homogeneity in two
ways and will address both. If the reviewer meant whether the droplet contains salt
nanocrystals upon reaching supersaturation, hence making the solvation environment
inhomogeneous, then we can confidently say that this does not occur. If such salt
crystals exist, they would serve as nucleation sites, causing the salt in the droplet to
crystalize and the droplet will no longer be aqueous. Because we were able to measure
the Mie resonances coming from the droplet under IR irradiation (Figure 3B), the
droplet remains aqueous, hence the ions are under a homogenous solvation
environment.
If the reviewer meant whether the droplet contains the same salt content as it
undergoes light-induced evaporation/condensation, we can also confidently say that this
is true because salt crystals cannot evaporate from the droplet. While the droplet is
undergoing further evaporation upon IR irradiation at peak absorbance (2053 cm-1),
hence becoming even more supersaturated, the droplet remained aqueous (Figure 3B).
Therefore, we can conclude that the droplet retained the same salt composition
throughout the optical measurement period. To clarify these points, we have included
the following in the manuscript:
Another concern is whether the droplet remains homogenous during the evaporation/condensation
process. Previous studies31,32 have shown that NaCl microdroplets can remain aqueous until 40%
RH before crystallizing, hence we do not foresee the existence of salt crashing out of the droplet,
causing inhomogeneity in the solvation environment. Additionally, salt cannot evaporate from the
droplet, hence as moisture condenses back onto the droplet after IR irradiation, we expect the salt
composition of the droplet to remain the same.
